questions.q: Why does a protocol still need phased rollout protections even after passing an audit and launching a bug bounty?
options: Neither an audit nor a bug bounty reduces risk to zero -- mainnet with real users is the first environment that tests assumptions nobody thought to question
Audits and bug bounties guarantee a contract has zero remaining bugs
Phased rollouts are only useful for protocols that skip an audit entirely
Bug bounties eliminate the need for any deposit limits once active
questions.explain: An audit and a bounty both reduce but don't eliminate risk; phasing the rollout limits what an undiscovered issue could actually cost.

questions.q: In the example deposit function, what does the require() check actually enforce?
options: That totalDeposits plus the incoming amount stays under depositCap, or the transaction reverts
That only the contract owner can ever call the deposit function
That the deposit amount is always exactly equal to depositCap
That withdrawals are permanently disabled for all users
questions.explain: The cap is enforced on-chain -- any deposit that would push total deposits over the cap simply reverts, bounding the contract's maximum exposure.

questions.q: What is an example of 'feature flagging' as a phasing technique, according to this lesson?
options: Shipping deposits first and enabling withdrawals only once deposits have run cleanly, narrowing what's exposed at any one time
Enabling every contract function simultaneously on day one with no restrictions
Only allowing the original deployer to ever use the contract
Disabling the bug bounty program once feature flags are in place
questions.explain: Feature flagging narrows the exposed surface by enabling functionality incrementally, rather than all at once.

questions.q: What should actually trigger raising a deposit cap, according to this lesson?
options: Evidence that real usage has run cleanly with no incidents -- not simply the passage of a fixed amount of calendar time
A fixed two-week countdown that applies regardless of actual usage
A single engineer's decision made independently of any approval process
The cap should never be raised under any circumstances
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly argues for raising caps based on evidence of clean real-world usage, not a calendar schedule.

questions.q: What approval path does this lesson say should be used to raise a deposit cap?
options: The same multisig approval path established in Chapter 3, Lesson 16 -- not one person's judgment call
Any single team member can raise the cap unilaterally at any time
Raising the cap requires no approval process of any kind
Only the original auditor from Lesson 27 can authorize a cap increase
questions.explain: Consistent with the course's multisig-control theme, raising the cap should go through the same shared approval process as deployment and upgrades.
